angle: compound interest explained in 20 lessons, from 3 angles: numbers, psychology, playbook
title: Compound Interest Explained: The 8th Wonder of the World

scenes.text: Hi, I'm Ryan Rover. You've probably heard the quote. Compound interest is the eighth wonder of the world. He who understands it, earns it. He who doesn't, pays it. It's usually credited to Albert Einstein. Here's a fun fact. There's no good evidence Einstein ever said it. But whoever said it was right. Compound interest is the most powerful force in personal finance. It can make ordinary people wealthy, and it can keep ordinary people broke. Today, we're going to explain it completely, in twenty lessons, so it works for you instead of against you.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: Here's compound interest in one picture. Would you rather have one million dollars today, or a single penny that doubles every day for thirty days? On day thirty, the penny is worth more than five million dollars.

card.note: One cent doubled every day: day 30 = $5,368,709.12

scenes.short_hook: Einstein probably never said this. But it's still true.

scenes.text: The penny puzzle shows the strange thing about compounding. For most of the month, the penny looks pathetic. On day ten, it's worth about five dollars. On day twenty, about five thousand. Then it explodes. Most of the growth happens at the very end. That's exactly how compound interest works with real money, just over years instead of days. The early years feel slow and almost pointless. The later years feel like magic. And most people quit before the magic starts.
scenes.caption: SLOW, THEN SUDDEN

scenes.text: We'll explain compounding from three angles. First, the numbers. How it actually works, the rule of seventy two, compounding frequency and the real math behind famous examples. Second, the psychology. Why our brains struggle to understand exponential growth, and how that costs us money. And third, the playbook. How to put compounding to work in your life, and how to stop it working against you. Quick note. Growth examples use stated returns like seven percent. Those are illustrations, not promises.
scenes.caption: THREE ANGLES

scenes.text: Let's start at the very beginning. What is compound interest, exactly?
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: Our sources. The Einstein quote's history comes from quote researchers like the Quote Investigator, which found no reliable source. Benjamin Franklin's bequest comes from historical records of the Franklin trusts in Boston and Philadelphia. Research on how people misunderstand compounding comes from economists Victor Stango and Jonathan Zinman, and from financial literacy research by Annamaria Lusardi and Olivia Mitchell. Credit card rates come from the Federal Reserve. This is education, not financial advice.
scenes.caption: OUR SOURCES

scenes.text: Angle one. The numbers. Seven lessons on how compounding really works.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: Lesson number one. The difference between simple and compound interest.
scenes.caption: LESSON 1

scenes.text: Simple interest is paid only on your original amount. Put one thousand dollars in an account paying ten percent simple interest, and you earn one hundred dollars every year. After ten years, you have two thousand dollars. Steady, predictable, and kind of boring.
scenes.caption: SIMPLE INTEREST

scenes.text: Compound interest is paid on your original amount plus all the interest you've already earned. The same one thousand dollars at ten percent compounded yearly becomes one thousand one hundred after year one, then one thousand two hundred ten, then one thousand three hundred thirty one. After ten years, it's about two thousand five hundred ninety four dollars. Almost six hundred dollars more than simple interest, without adding a cent.
scenes.caption: INTEREST ON INTEREST

scenes.text: Over longer periods, the gap becomes enormous. After thirty years, simple interest gives you four thousand dollars. Compound interest at ten percent gives you over seventeen thousand. Same starting money, same rate. The only difference is that the interest itself starts earning interest.
scenes.caption: THE GAP GROWS

scenes.text: Remember it this way. Simple interest is a staircase. Compound interest is a snowball. The staircase climbs the same step every year. The snowball picks up more snow the bigger it gets.
scenes.caption: STAIRCASE VS SNOWBALL

scenes.text: Lesson number two. The rule of seventy two.
scenes.caption: LESSON 2

scenes.text: Here's the most useful shortcut in personal finance. Divide seventy two by your yearly return, and you get roughly how many years it takes for money to double. At six percent, about twelve years. At eight percent, about nine years. At twelve percent, about six years. It's an estimate, but it's remarkably close for typical rates.
scenes.caption: 72 ÷ RATE = YEARS
scenes.short_hook: Divide seventy two by this number and see how fast money doubles.

scenes.text: The rule works for anything that grows at a steady rate. Investments, debt, even inflation. At three percent inflation, prices double in about twenty four years. At twenty four percent credit card interest, an unpaid balance can double in about three years.
scenes.caption: IT WORKS FOR DEBT TOO

scenes.text: Now think in doublings. At seven percent, money doubles roughly every ten years. Ten thousand dollars at age thirty could become about twenty thousand at forty, forty thousand at fifty, and eighty thousand at sixty. Each decade, the jump is bigger than the last.
scenes.caption: 10K, 20K, 40K, 80K

scenes.text: Try this. Take your savings account rate and divide seventy two by it. If the answer is fifty years or more, your money is barely growing. Then try it with your credit card rate, and see how fast debt can double.
scenes.caption: TRY YOUR OWN RATES

scenes.text: Here's the doubling in action. Ten thousand dollars at a seven percent average yearly return, roughly doubles about every ten years. After thirty years, it's about eighty one thousand dollars, without adding a single dollar.

card.note: Illustration, compounded monthly. Returns are not guaranteed.

scenes.text: Lesson number three. How often interest compounds matters, a little.
scenes.caption: LESSON 3

scenes.text: Interest can compound yearly, monthly or even daily. The more often it compounds, the faster the balance grows, because interest starts earning interest sooner. Twelve percent compounded monthly is slightly more than twelve percent compounded yearly.
scenes.caption: HOW OFTEN?

scenes.text: That's why banks show two numbers. The annual percentage rate, or APR, is the simple yearly rate. The annual percentage yield, or APY, includes the effect of compounding. On savings, compare APYs. On debt, remember that the effective cost can be a little higher than the APR, because interest compounds.
scenes.caption: APR VS APY

scenes.text: Most credit cards calculate interest daily, using a daily rate based on the APR. So a card at twenty four percent charges roughly six and a half hundredths of a percent every single day on your balance, and that interest becomes part of the balance.
scenes.caption: CARDS COMPOUND DAILY

scenes.text: In practice, frequency matters much less than rate and time. Don't obsess over daily versus monthly. Focus on getting a good rate on savings, a low rate on debt, and as much time as possible.
scenes.caption: RATE AND TIME MATTER MORE

scenes.text: Lesson number four. Regular contributions supercharge compounding.
scenes.caption: LESSON 4

scenes.text: A single deposit compounds nicely. But adding money every month is where compounding really shines. Each new deposit starts its own little snowball. Over the years, you're rolling hundreds of snowballs at once.
scenes.caption: HUNDREDS OF SNOWBALLS

scenes.text: Two hundred dollars a month for thirty years at a seven percent average yearly return grows to roughly two hundred forty four thousand dollars. You contribute seventy two thousand. The other one hundred seventy two thousand is growth.
scenes.caption: $72K IN, $244K OUT

scenes.text: Notice that in the early years, your contributions are most of the balance. Somewhere around year fifteen or twenty in this example, yearly growth starts to rival what you add each year. After that, the money is doing more work than you are.
scenes.caption: THE CROSSOVER POINT

scenes.text: Try this. Set up an automatic monthly investment, even small. Then look up the year when your yearly growth might exceed your yearly contributions. That's a milestone worth celebrating.
scenes.caption: FIND YOUR CROSSOVER

scenes.text: Two hundred dollars a month for thirty years, at a seven percent average yearly return, grows to roughly two hundred forty four thousand dollars. Total contributed, seventy two thousand.
Lesson number five. Benjamin Franklin's two hundred year experiment.
scenes.caption: LESSON 5

scenes.text: When Benjamin Franklin died in seventeen ninety, he left one thousand pounds each to the cities of Boston and Philadelphia, with instructions to lend the money to young tradesmen at interest and let it grow for two hundred years. It was a deliberate demonstration of compounding.
scenes.caption: FRANKLIN'S GIFT

scenes.text: Part of the money was released after one hundred years, as Franklin instructed. The rest kept growing. By nineteen ninety, the funds had grown into millions of dollars. Boston's fund was worth around five million, and Philadelphia's around two million, according to historical accounts.
scenes.caption: MILLIONS BY 1990

scenes.text: The returns weren't spectacular, and the funds faced management problems over the centuries. But even modest growth, given two hundred years, turned a gift into a fortune. Time can make up for a lot.
scenes.caption: TIME MAKES UP FOR A LOT

scenes.text: The lesson for us. We don't have two hundred years. But we might have forty or fifty. That's plenty of time for compounding to do something remarkable.
scenes.caption: YOU HAVE DECADES

scenes.text: Lesson number six. Why most of Warren Buffett's fortune came late in life.
scenes.caption: LESSON 6

scenes.text: Warren Buffett is one of the most successful investors in history. But as writer Morgan Housel points out in The Psychology of Money, the vast majority of Buffett's net worth was accumulated after his sixty fifth birthday.
scenes.caption: AFTER AGE 65
scenes.short_hook: Most of Warren Buffett's fortune came after he turned sixty five.

scenes.text: Buffett started investing as a child and never stopped. His skill matters, of course. But Housel argues the real secret is time. Buffett has been compounding for more than eighty years.
scenes.caption: 80 YEARS OF COMPOUNDING

scenes.text: Housel makes the point that if Buffett had started at thirty and retired at sixty, he'd be wealthy, but nowhere near as famous. The extra decades at both ends made the difference.
scenes.caption: THE EXTRA DECADES

scenes.text: For regular people, the lesson is simple. Start as early as you can, and stay invested as long as you can.
scenes.caption: START EARLY, STAY LONG

scenes.text: Lesson number seven. Compounding works against you when you owe money.
scenes.caption: LESSON 7

scenes.text: Everything we've said about growth applies to debt in reverse. The Federal Reserve reports average credit card rates above twenty percent for accounts paying interest. At those rates, unpaid balances grow quickly.
scenes.caption: DEBT COMPOUNDS

scenes.text: If you only make the minimum payment, it can take many years to pay off a balance, and the total interest can be a large share of the original amount. Credit card statements are required to show this.
scenes.caption: YEARS OF PAYMENTS

scenes.text: This is why the quote ends the way it does. He who understands it, earns it. He who doesn't, pays it.
scenes.caption: EARN IT OR PAY IT

scenes.text: Try this. Find the minimum payment warning box on your card statement. It shows how long payoff takes at the minimum.
scenes.caption: READ THE BOX

scenes.text: That's angle one. Simple versus compound, the rule of seventy two, frequency, monthly contributions, Franklin's experiment, Buffett's late fortune, and compounding debt. Now angle two. The psychology. Why our brains get this so wrong.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: Humans evolved in a world of straight lines. If you walk twice as far, it takes about twice as long. If you gather twice as many berries, you have twice as much food. Exponential growth is unnatural for our brains, and that's why compounding surprises nearly everyone. In this angle, we'll look at seven ways our psychology gets in the way of compounding, and what to do about each one.
scenes.caption: BRAINS THINK IN STRAIGHT LINES

scenes.text: Lesson number eight. Exponential growth bias.
scenes.caption: LESSON 8

scenes.text: Economists Victor Stango and Jonathan Zinman studied what they called exponential growth bias. When people are asked to estimate how something grows at a steady percentage, they tend to imagine a straight line instead of a curve. So they badly underestimate long term growth, on both savings and debt.
scenes.caption: THE BIAS

scenes.text: Their research found that households with stronger bias tended to borrow more at high rates and save less. That makes sense. If you think a credit card balance grows slowly, borrowing feels cheap. If you think savings grow slowly, saving feels pointless. Underestimating compounding costs money on both sides of the ledger.
scenes.caption: IT COSTS MONEY TWICE

scenes.text: The penny puzzle from the beginning works because it shocks this bias. Almost nobody guesses that a penny doubled for thirty days ends up above five million dollars. Our intuition simply isn't built for doubling. That's not a personal failing. It's how human brains work, which is why we need tools instead of gut feelings.
scenes.caption: NOBODY GUESSES RIGHT

scenes.text: Try this. Before calculating, guess what one hundred dollars a month becomes in forty years at seven percent. Write your guess down. Then check it with a calculator. The real answer is roughly two hundred sixty thousand dollars. Most people guess far too low, and that gap is the cost of straight line thinking.
scenes.caption: GUESS, THEN CHECK

scenes.text: Lesson number nine. The boring middle.
scenes.caption: LESSON 9

scenes.text: In the first years of investing, growth is tiny. After five years of one hundred dollars a month at seven percent, you might have around seven thousand dollars, and most of that is your own money. The growth part might be about a thousand dollars. It honestly feels like nothing is happening.
scenes.caption: NOTHING IS HAPPENING

scenes.text: This is where many people quit. They stop contributing, cash out for something more exciting, or switch strategies every few months. They leave right before the curve starts bending upward, which means they do all the hard, slow work and miss the rewarding part.
scenes.caption: QUITTING TOO EARLY

scenes.text: Think back to the penny. On day ten, it's worth about five dollars. On day twenty, about five thousand. On day thirty, more than five million. If you'd judged the penny on day ten, you'd have called it a failure. The boring middle isn't a sign that compounding isn't working. It's a normal part of how compounding works.
scenes.caption: DAY 10 VS DAY 30

scenes.text: Try this. For the first five years, measure your success by the habit, not the balance. Did the automatic investment happen every month? Did you raise it when you got a raise? If yes, you're winning, even if the balance looks small. The balance will take care of itself later.
scenes.caption: TRACK THE HABIT

scenes.text: Lesson number ten. Impatience leads people to chase faster returns.
scenes.caption: LESSON 10

scenes.text: Because normal compounding is slow at first, people look for shortcuts. Hot stocks, trendy coins, leveraged bets, get rich quick schemes. The promise of fast returns is especially tempting when steady growth feels painfully slow. And social media is full of people showing off their wins, but rarely their losses.
scenes.caption: CHASING SPEED

scenes.text: Here's the math that makes chasing so dangerous. Big losses destroy compounding. Lose fifty percent, and you need a one hundred percent gain just to get back to where you started. Lose eighty percent, and you need a four hundred percent gain. Avoiding large losses matters just as much as earning good returns, maybe more.
scenes.caption: -50% NEEDS +100%

scenes.text: That's why so many successful long term investors emphasize steady, diversified investing over chasing big wins. A portfolio that grows steadily without huge crashes often ends up ahead of one that soars and collapses. Slow and steady compounding tends to beat boom and bust.
scenes.caption: SLOW AND STEADY

scenes.text: Try this. Keep your core long term investments boring and diversified, like broad index funds. If you really want to speculate, set aside a small amount you can afford to lose completely, and never add to it after a loss.
scenes.caption: BORING CORE, SMALL FUN BUCKET

scenes.text: Quick pause. If compounding is finally clicking for you, please subscribe to Ryan Rover Money. It's free, and it helps us keep explaining money in plain English. Now, lesson eleven.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: Lesson number eleven. Present bias works against compounding.
scenes.caption: LESSON 11

scenes.text: Compounding rewards patience, but our brains are wired to prefer rewards right now. Spending one hundred dollars today on something fun feels much more real than having several hundred dollars more in thirty years. Economists call this present bias, and it's one of the strongest forces in personal finance.
scenes.caption: NOW FEELS BETTER

scenes.text: That's exactly why automatic investing works so well. You make the decision once, when you're calm and thinking about the long term. After that, the money moves before present bias ever gets a vote. You don't have to win the battle with temptation every month, because there's no battle.
scenes.caption: DECIDE ONCE

scenes.text: Picturing your future self also helps. Research by Hal Hershfield and colleagues found that people who viewed digitally aged images of themselves were more willing to save for the future. When the future version of you feels like a real person, saving feels less like losing money and more like helping someone you care about.
scenes.caption: MEET FUTURE YOU

scenes.text: Try this. Write down exactly what your investments are for. Not just retirement, but something specific. Freedom to leave a job you dislike. A paid off home. Retiring at sixty. Specific goals make the future feel close enough to fight for.
scenes.caption: WRITE IT DOWN

scenes.text: Lesson number twelve. Interrupting compounding is very expensive.
scenes.caption: LESSON 12

scenes.text: Charlie Munger, Warren Buffett's longtime business partner, put it simply. The first rule of compounding is never to interrupt it unnecessarily. Cashing out early, stopping contributions for years, or panic selling during a crash all break the chain, and the chain is where the magic lives.
scenes.caption: NEVER INTERRUPT IT

scenes.text: Early withdrawals from retirement accounts are a common interruption. Depending on the account and your situation, withdrawing before retirement age can trigger income taxes and a penalty, and the money withdrawn loses all its future compounding. A ten thousand dollar withdrawal at thirty could cost far more than ten thousand dollars by retirement.
scenes.caption: EARLY WITHDRAWALS COST

scenes.text: Job changes are another. When people leave a job, many cash out their old four oh one k instead of rolling it over, especially when the balance is small. It feels like free money. But it often means taxes, penalties, and starting the snowball over from zero.
scenes.caption: ROLL IT OVER

scenes.text: Try this. If you change jobs, roll your old retirement account into an IRA or your new employer's plan. And keep an emergency fund, so a surprise expense never forces you to break the chain.
scenes.caption: DON'T CASH OUT

scenes.text: Lesson number thirteen. Most people misunderstand compounding.
scenes.caption: LESSON 13

scenes.text: Economists Annamaria Lusardi and Olivia Mitchell created three simple questions to measure financial literacy. One asks about compound interest, one about inflation, and one about diversification. In surveys over many years, a large share of American adults couldn't answer all three correctly.
scenes.caption: THE BIG THREE QUESTIONS

scenes.text: Their research found that people who answered correctly were more likely to plan for retirement, invest and avoid high cost borrowing. In other words, understanding concepts like compounding is linked with better financial outcomes, not just better test scores.
scenes.caption: KNOWLEDGE PAYS

scenes.text: The encouraging part is that compounding isn't hard to learn. If you've watched this far, you now understand more about it than many adults ever will. You know the difference between simple and compound interest, the rule of seventy two, and why time matters so much.
scenes.caption: NOW YOU KNOW

scenes.text: Try this. Explain the rule of seventy two to a friend, partner or child this week. Teaching is one of the best ways to remember something, and you might change their financial future too.
scenes.caption: TEACH SOMEONE

scenes.text: Lesson number fourteen. Small differences in rate become huge over time.
scenes.caption: LESSON 14

scenes.text: One percent sounds tiny. But compounding magnifies small differences. Over decades, a one percent difference in your yearly return, whether it comes from fees, investment choices or idle cash, can change your final balance dramatically.
scenes.caption: 1% MATTERS

scenes.text: Here's an example. Five hundred dollars a month for forty years at seven percent grows to roughly one point three million dollars. At six percent, it's roughly one million. That single percentage point is worth around three hundred thousand dollars in this example.
scenes.caption: 6% VS 7% OVER 40 YEARS

scenes.text: That's why investment fees matter so much. Unlike market returns, fees are certain. They come out every year, in good markets and bad. Choosing a fund with a fee of one percent instead of a small fraction of a percent is effectively choosing a lower return for decades.
scenes.caption: FEES ARE CERTAIN

scenes.text: Try this. List every fund you own and its expense ratio. If any are around one percent or higher, check whether a lower cost alternative exists in the same category.
scenes.caption: LOWER YOUR FEES

scenes.text: That's angle two. Straight line thinking, the boring middle, impatience, present bias, interruptions, the literacy gap and small rate differences. Now angle three. The playbook.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: Now let's turn knowledge into action. Here are six moves that put compounding to work for you, and stop it working against you. None of them require a big income, special skills or perfect timing. They just require starting, and then staying out of compounding's way.
scenes.caption: SIX MOVES

scenes.text: Move number fifteen. Start now, with whatever you have.
scenes.caption: LESSON 15

scenes.text: The single biggest factor in compounding is time. Every year you wait is a year of growth you never get back, and those early years are the ones that compound the longest. A dollar invested at twenty five has roughly forty years to grow. A dollar invested at fifty five has about ten.
scenes.caption: TIME IS THE MULTIPLIER

scenes.text: You don't need much. Many brokerages offer accounts with no minimums and fractional shares of broad index funds. Fifty or one hundred dollars a month, in a tax advantaged account like a four oh one k or an IRA, is a real start.
scenes.caption: START SMALL

scenes.text: You can always increase the amount later, when your income grows or debts are paid off. What you can never do is go back and start earlier. That's why the best time to start is always as soon as possible.
scenes.caption: YOU CAN'T START EARLIER

scenes.text: Try this. Open an account and set up your first automatic investment this week, even if it's small. Then set a calendar reminder to increase it in six months.
scenes.caption: THIS WEEK

scenes.text: Move number sixteen. Eliminate high interest debt.
scenes.caption: LESSON 16

scenes.text: Paying off a credit card at twenty percent is like earning a guaranteed twenty percent return, something no investment reliably offers. Before compounding can work for you, it helps to stop it working against you.
scenes.caption: GUARANTEED RETURN

scenes.text: A simple method is to list every debt by interest rate, pay the minimum on all of them, and put every extra dollar on the highest rate. When that one's gone, roll its payment into the next one. Each payoff makes the next one faster.
scenes.caption: HIGHEST RATE FIRST

scenes.text: Once the high interest debt is gone, redirect those same monthly payments into investing. Now the snowball rolls in your direction. The money that used to compound for the bank starts compounding for you.
scenes.caption: FLIP THE SNOWBALL

scenes.text: Try this. Stop adding new charges to any card that carries a balance. Use a debit card or cash for everyday spending until the balance is gone.
scenes.caption: STOP ADDING

scenes.text: Move number seventeen. Reinvest dividends and interest.
scenes.caption: LESSON 17

scenes.text: Dividends and interest are the fuel of compounding. When a company pays a dividend and you spend it, the snowball stops growing. When you reinvest it, it buys more shares, which pay more dividends, which buy more shares.
scenes.caption: REINVEST

scenes.text: Most brokerages let you automatically reinvest dividends, often called a DRIP, short for dividend reinvestment plan. For long term money, turning it on is one of the easiest ways to keep compounding running at full speed.
scenes.caption: TURN ON DRIP

scenes.text: Historical data from S and P Dow Jones Indices shows that reinvested dividends have made up a significant share of the S and P five hundred's total return over long periods. Investors who spent their dividends saw much less growth than those who reinvested them.
scenes.caption: DIVIDENDS ADD UP

scenes.text: Try this. Log into your accounts and check that dividend reinvestment is turned on for your long term investments.
scenes.caption: CHECK IT

scenes.text: Move number eighteen. Keep investment costs low.
scenes.caption: LESSON 18

scenes.text: Every dollar paid in fees is a dollar that stops compounding for you, along with all the growth it would have produced. Over decades, that adds up. Fees are one of the few parts of investing you can fully control.
scenes.caption: FEES STOP COMPOUNDING

scenes.text: Low cost broad index funds often charge a small fraction of a percent per year. Many actively managed funds charge much more, and research such as the SPIVA reports has found that most of them underperformed their benchmarks over long periods after fees.
scenes.caption: LOW COST FUNDS

scenes.text: If you work with an advisor, that can be valuable, but know exactly what you pay and how they're paid. A fee only fiduciary is required to act in your best interest.
scenes.caption: KNOW WHAT YOU PAY

scenes.text: Try this. Add up your total yearly investment fees in dollars, not percentages. Seeing the dollar amount often motivates a change.
scenes.caption: FEES IN DOLLARS

scenes.text: Move number nineteen. Automate, then mostly ignore it.
scenes.caption: LESSON 19

scenes.text: The best compounders often do the least. They set up automatic investing into diversified, low cost funds, and then they leave it alone for years. No constant trading, no reacting to headlines, no switching strategies every time something new is popular.
scenes.caption: THE LAZY ADVANTAGE
scenes.short_hook: The secret to compounding? Do almost nothing for a very long time.

scenes.text: Research by Brad Barber and Terrance Odean found that individual investors who traded most frequently earned lower returns after costs than those who traded less. Activity often feels productive, but with investing, it frequently interrupts compounding.
scenes.caption: TRADING LESS WINS

scenes.text: A simple routine works for most people. Review your accounts once or twice a year. Rebalance if your mix has drifted far from your plan. Raise your contributions when you can. Otherwise, let time do its work.
scenes.caption: REVIEW TWICE A YEAR

scenes.text: Try this. Turn off daily price notifications from your investing app, and move the app off your home screen.
scenes.caption: NOTIFICATIONS OFF

scenes.text: Move number twenty. Compound your skills, health and relationships too.
scenes.caption: LESSON 20

scenes.text: Compounding isn't only about money. Skills build on skills. Knowledge builds on knowledge. Trust in relationships builds over years. A little improvement every day, kept up for decades, can produce enormous results.
scenes.caption: SKILLS COMPOUND

scenes.text: Reading thirty minutes a day adds up to many books a year. Exercising regularly protects your health, which protects your ability to earn. Learning a valuable skill can raise your income for the rest of your career.
scenes.caption: SMALL DAILY HABITS

scenes.text: And these forms of compounding feed your financial compounding. A higher income lets you invest more, which compounds faster. Better health means more working years and fewer medical bills. It's a double snowball.
scenes.caption: A DOUBLE SNOWBALL

scenes.text: Try this. Pick one skill that could raise your income, and spend fifteen minutes a day on it this month. Fifteen minutes a day is over ninety hours a year.
scenes.caption: 15 MINUTES A DAY

scenes.text: Here's a classic example that shows compounding's power.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: Saver one invests two hundred dollars a month from age twenty five to thirty five, then stops completely. That's ten years and twenty four thousand dollars. Saver two starts at thirty five and invests two hundred dollars a month until sixty five. That's thirty years and seventy two thousand dollars.
scenes.caption: TWO SAVERS
scenes.short_hook: Ten years of saving beat thirty years. Here's how.

scenes.text: At a seven percent average yearly return, who has more at sixty five? Saver one. The money invested early had thirty extra years to compound, and that head start is enough to beat three times the contributions in this example. Time beat money.
scenes.caption: TIME BEAT MONEY

scenes.text: Of course, the best plan is to start early and keep going. But if you take away one idea from this video, let it be this. The dollars you invest early are the most powerful dollars you'll ever invest.
scenes.caption: EARLY DOLLARS ARE POWERFUL

scenes.text: Let's make this personal. Here's what compounding looks like depending on when you start. Same habit for everyone, three hundred dollars a month, a seven percent average yearly return. Remember, this is an illustration, not a promise.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: Start at twenty five and keep going until sixty five. That's forty years. Three hundred dollars a month grows to roughly seven hundred eighty thousand dollars. You contributed one hundred forty four thousand. The other six hundred thousand or so is growth. Compounding did most of the work, not you.
scenes.caption: AGE 25: ABOUT $787K

scenes.text: Start at thirty five. Thirty years of the same habit grows to roughly three hundred sixty six thousand dollars. That's still a very real retirement cushion, but notice something. Waiting just ten years cut the final number by more than half. That's the cost of delay, in one sentence.
scenes.query: Person in their thirties with family
scenes.caption: AGE 35: ABOUT $366K

scenes.text: Start at forty five. Twenty years grows to roughly one hundred fifty six thousand dollars. Start at fifty five, and ten years grows to roughly fifty two thousand. Less dramatic, but still meaningful. And people who start later often earn more, so they can invest more each month to make up some of the gap.
scenes.caption: AGE 45: $156K, AGE 55: $52K

scenes.text: Here's the catch up math. If you start at forty and invest one thousand dollars a month for twenty five years at the same seven percent, you could reach roughly eight hundred ten thousand dollars. So a late start isn't hopeless. It just means time is scarcer, so your contributions have to work harder.
scenes.caption: CATCHING UP IS POSSIBLE

scenes.text: And in the United States, people fifty and older are generally allowed extra catch up contributions in retirement accounts like four oh one ks and IRAs. The limits change, so check the current numbers on the IRS website. The rules were written with late starters in mind.
scenes.caption: CATCH UP CONTRIBUTIONS

scenes.text: Question one. Do savings accounts compound? Yes, most pay compound interest, usually daily or monthly. But rates on many traditional savings accounts are low. High yield savings accounts usually pay more.
scenes.caption: DO SAVINGS COMPOUND?

scenes.text: Question two. Do stocks compound? Stocks don't pay a set interest rate, but they compound through rising company values and reinvested dividends. That's why long term stock investing is often described as compounding.
scenes.caption: DO STOCKS COMPOUND?

scenes.text: Question three. Is it too late to benefit from compounding? No. Even ten or twenty years of compounding can make a big difference. Start now and invest as much as you reasonably can.
scenes.caption: TOO LATE?

scenes.text: Question four. Does inflation cancel out compounding? It works against it. Inflation slowly shrinks what each dollar can buy. At three percent inflation, five thousand dollars twenty years from now buys roughly what two thousand eight hundred dollars buys today. That's why money that must grow for decades usually needs to earn more than inflation.
scenes.caption: INFLATION FIGHTS BACK

scenes.text: Question five. What's the difference between APR and APY? APR is the yearly rate before compounding is counted. APY, the annual percentage yield, includes compounding. So when you're saving, compare APYs. And when you're borrowing, remember that the true cost of a card with a twenty four percent APR is even a little higher once compounding kicks in.
scenes.caption: APR VS APY

scenes.text: Question six. Should I pay off my mortgage or invest? It depends on your rate, your taxes and your peace of mind. Generally, the higher your mortgage rate, the more paying it down acts like a guaranteed return. Many people do both. A low rate mortgage is very different from a twenty percent credit card.
scenes.caption: MORTGAGE OR INVEST?

scenes.text: Question seven. How do I know my real return? Most brokerages show a personal rate of return in your account. Look for it, and compare it to a simple broad index fund over the same period. If you're far behind, high fees or too much trading may be the reason.
scenes.caption: KNOW YOUR REAL RETURN

scenes.text: Question eight. Can compounding work with very small amounts? Absolutely. Twenty five dollars a month won't make you rich on its own, but it builds the habit, and habits are what grow. Many people who start tiny raise the amount over the years as income grows. The habit you build at twenty five dollars is the same habit that later moves two thousand.
scenes.caption: SMALL AMOUNTS COUNT

scenes.text: Question nine. What if the market crashes right after I start? Crashes happen, and they're painful. But for someone investing every month, a falling market means buying more shares at lower prices. Historically, broad markets have recovered from past crashes over time, though there's never a guarantee, and recovery can take years.
scenes.caption: WHAT ABOUT CRASHES?

scenes.text: Mistake one. Keeping long term money in cash for years. Cash is great for an emergency fund and short term goals. But money you won't need for decades, sitting in an account earning far less than inflation, loses buying power every single year. Know which money is for safety, and which money is for growth.
scenes.caption: MISTAKE 1: TOO MUCH CASH

scenes.text: Mistake two. Waiting for the perfect moment. People wait for the market to drop, for a raise, for the new year, for less stress. Meanwhile, months turn into years. Nobody can reliably predict the market, and the perfect moment rarely announces itself. A steady monthly habit removes the guessing completely.
scenes.caption: MISTAKE 2: WAITING

scenes.text: Mistake three. Ignoring the reverse snowball. Some people invest diligently while carrying credit card balances at twenty percent or more. The debt often compounds faster than the investments grow. Fixing that first is one of the highest return moves most people will ever make.
scenes.query: Credit card bill and investment app
scenes.caption: MISTAKE 3: IGNORING DEBT

scenes.text: Avoid those three, follow the playbook, and give it time. That's honestly most of what compounding asks of you. It's simple, but it isn't easy, because it asks for patience in a world that rewards speed.
scenes.caption: SIMPLE, NOT EASY

scenes.text: Quick recap. Angle one, the numbers. Simple versus compound, the rule of seventy two, compounding frequency, monthly contributions, Franklin's experiment, Buffett's late fortune, and compounding debt.
scenes.caption: THE NUMBERS: 1 TO 7

scenes.text: Angle two, the psychology. Exponential growth bias, the boring middle, impatience, present bias, interruptions, the literacy gap, and small rate differences.
scenes.caption: THE PSYCHOLOGY: 8 TO 14

scenes.text: Angle three, the playbook. Start now, kill compounding debt, reinvest everything, lower your costs, automate and ignore, and compound yourself too.
scenes.caption: THE PLAYBOOK: 15 TO 20

See you in the next one.
